Arrays.description: A contiguous block of memory storing elements of the same type, accessed by index in O(1).
common_misconceptions: Believing array indexing is not constant time.
Confusing array length with allocated capacity.
key_ideas: Random access via index is O(1).
Insertion/deletion in the middle is O(n).
Arrays are the base building block for many other structures.
examples: arr = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]; arr[2] returns 4 instantly, regardless of array size.

Pointers.description: A pointer/reference stores the memory address of another value, enabling indirection and linked structures.
common_misconceptions: Believing a pointer holds a copy of the value instead of an address.
Confusing a null pointer with an empty value.
key_ideas: A pointer lets one structure refer to another without copying data.
Following ('dereferencing') a pointer retrieves the value it points to.
Linked structures like linked lists and trees are built from pointers.
examples: node.next points to the memory address of the following node in a linked list.

Linked Lists.description: A sequence of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next node, allowing O(1) insertion/deletion at known positions.
common_misconceptions: Assuming linked lists support O(1) random access like arrays.
Forgetting to update pointers when inserting/deleting, causing broken chains.
key_ideas: No contiguous memory requirement, unlike arrays.
Traversal is O(n); random access is O(n).
Insertion/deletion at a known node is O(1).
examples: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> None; inserting 5 after 1 only requires updating two pointers.

Recursion.description: A function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller subproblems until reaching a base case.
common_misconceptions: Forgetting the base case, causing infinite recursion.
Believing recursion is always less efficient than iteration.
key_ideas: Every recursive function needs a base case and a recursive case.
The call stack tracks pending calls, which is why DFS is naturally recursive.
Recursion trades explicit loops for implicit stack-based bookkeeping.
examples: factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1), with factorial(0) = 1 as the base case.

Trees.description: A hierarchical structure of nodes where each node has one parent (except the root) and zero or more children.
common_misconceptions: Confusing a tree with a general graph (trees have no cycles and exactly one path between any two nodes).
Assuming all trees are binary trees.
key_ideas: A tree is a special case of a graph: connected and acyclic.
Traversals (pre-order, in-order, post-order, level-order) visit nodes in different orders.
Level-order traversal of a tree is essentially BFS on a graph.
examples: A file system directory structure is a tree: folders contain files/subfolders, with one root.

Graphs.description: A set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges, which may be directed/undirected and weighted/unweighted.
common_misconceptions: Assuming graphs cannot have cycles.
Confusing directed and undirected edges.
Assuming every graph is connected.
key_ideas: Graphs generalize trees by allowing cycles and multiple paths.
Graphs can be represented as adjacency lists or adjacency matrices.
Traversal algorithms (BFS, DFS) are the foundation for almost all graph algorithms.
examples: A social network: people are nodes, friendships are edges.

BFS.description: Breadth-First Search explores a graph level by level from a source node, using a queue (FIFO) to guarantee nodes are visited in increasing distance from the source.
common_misconceptions: BFS uses a stack (this is DFS's mechanism, not BFS's).
BFS explores the deepest node first (this describes DFS).
BFS cannot find shortest paths (BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs by construction).
key_ideas: BFS uses a FIFO queue: the first node discovered is the first one expanded.
This guarantees nodes are visited in non-decreasing order of distance from the source.
Because of this ordering guarantee, BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph.
BFS is the conceptual ancestor of Dijkstra's algorithm, which generalizes BFS to weighted edges using a priority queue instead of a plain queue.
examples: Starting BFS from node A in A-B, A-C, B-D: visit order is A, then B and C (distance 1), then D (distance 2).

DFS.description: Depth-First Search explores a graph by going as deep as possible along a branch before backtracking, using a stack (explicit or via recursion).
common_misconceptions: DFS always finds the shortest path (DFS has no distance guarantee; it finds *a* path, not the shortest one).
DFS and BFS always visit nodes in the same order.
key_ideas: DFS uses a LIFO stack (explicit or the call stack via recursion).
DFS dives deep before exploring siblings, unlike BFS's level-by-level expansion.
DFS is well suited for tasks like cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components, not shortest-path guarantees.
examples: Starting DFS from node A in A-B, A-C, B-D: visit order could be A, B, D, C, going deep down one branch first.

Graph Traversal.description: The general concept of systematically visiting nodes in a graph, of which BFS and DFS are the two foundational strategies.
common_misconceptions: Believing there is only one 'correct' way to traverse a graph.
Not recognizing that traversal order affects which algorithmic guarantees hold (e.g. shortest-path guarantees only from BFS).
key_ideas: Traversal strategy determines what guarantees you get (shortest path, connectivity, ordering).
Choosing BFS vs DFS depends on the problem: shortest path in unweighted graphs favors BFS.
Traversal is the foundation for shortest-path algorithms like Dijkstra.
examples: Finding all nodes reachable from a source can use either BFS or DFS; finding the fewest-edges path requires BFS.

Shortest Paths.description: The problem of finding the minimum-cost path between nodes in a graph, where 'cost' is edge count (unweighted) or summed edge weights (weighted).
common_misconceptions: Assuming BFS solves shortest paths for weighted graphs too (BFS only guarantees shortest paths when all edges have equal weight).
Assuming any traversal order gives the shortest path.
key_ideas: In unweighted graphs, BFS directly gives the shortest path (fewest edges).
In weighted graphs, edge costs differ, so a plain queue no longer works — you need to always expand the currently-cheapest node.
This need motivates replacing BFS's queue with a priority queue, which is exactly what Dijkstra's algorithm does.
examples: In an unweighted graph, BFS from A finds node D in the fewest hops, which is the shortest path by edge count.

Dijkstra.description: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source node in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, by always expanding the closest unvisited node using a priority queue.
common_misconceptions: Dijkstra works with negative edges (it does not; negative weights break its greedy guarantee).
Dijkstra is unrelated to BFS (in fact, Dijkstra reduces to BFS when all edge weights are equal to 1).
Dijkstra explores nodes in insertion order rather than by cumulative distance.
key_ideas: Dijkstra is BFS generalized to weighted graphs: a priority queue (min-heap) replaces BFS's plain FIFO queue.
It greedily expands the unvisited node with the smallest known distance so far.
It requires non-negative edge weights to guarantee correctness.
Understanding why BFS guarantees shortest paths in unweighted graphs is the key intuition that transfers directly to understanding Dijkstra.
examples: In a weighted graph, Dijkstra maintains a running 'distance so far' for each node and always expands the node with the smallest tentative distance next.
